memory_candidates.content: When a script's own resolution-source/manifest file (e.g. check-module-invariants.sh's C15 anchor record) also gets scanned as a CITER in the same gate's citation walk, its own illustrative or changelog prose (e.g. examples of what an unresolved anchor would look like, or a `foo-*` glob shorthand) can be mistaken for real unresolved citations. Fix by excluding the resolution-source file itself from the citer walk (grep --exclude=<basename>), not by adding synthetic rows to the manifest for prose that isn't a real citation. Keep every other file, including sibling records of the same genre, in scope.

Under heavy multi-task concurrency in one working tree (multiple orchestrator dispatches editing shared hot files like a central check-module-invariants.sh or a widely-imported aggregator module), isolating only your own hunks via `git apply --cached` immediately before committing is necessary but not sufficient: a concurrent process can re-stage (git add) the full file again in the window between your isolation step and your own `git commit -- <pathspec>` call, which uses whatever is currently staged for that path rather than what you isolated moments earlier. The resulting commit is content-correct but attribution-mixed with the other task. There is no git-porcelain-level fix for this race; treat it as an expected, reportable hazard on heavily shared files rather than a bug in the isolation technique, and verify with `git show --stat <commit>` right after committing (not just before) to catch it.

On this environment's grep, `grep -rn <pattern> .` does NOT prefix matched paths with `./`, so a filter written as `grep -v '^\./specs/'` silently fails to exclude specs/** and lets those lines through. Use `grep -v '^specs/'` instead when excluding a directory from a repo-root-relative recursive grep on this system.
